docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Eventify documentation

docs.title: Event sourcing on Kafka, in plain Java
docs.text:
You write commands, events and handlers. Eventify stores every event in Kafka, rebuilds an aggregate's state when a command arrives and passes new events on to whoever reacts to them. No database, no extra server.

Get started → Spring Boot

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1 Send a command

PlaceOrder goes to the aggregate's command topic, keyed by its id.

2 Decide

A @CommandHandler gets the current state and returns events, or rejects the command.

3 Record

The events are stored and published in one transaction. @EventSourcingHandler methods build the next state.

4 React

@EventHandler methods update views, send mail or return the next command.

docs.title: Guides
docs.text: Getting started → A first aggregate, from dependency to running application. Domain modeling → Aggregates, commands and events. Handlers → Decide on commands, build state and react to events. Command gateway → Send and schedule commands, and wait for their result. Spring Boot → The starter, handler beans and @KafkaListener. Testing → Given, when, then: without a broker.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Keep aggregates, commands and events immutable.
  • Use the aggregate id as the command key.
  • Keep event-sourcing handlers deterministic and free of side effects.
  • Enable snapshots only when replaying a long history becomes expensive. With deleteEvents = true, history before a snapshot is gone.

docs.title: Snapshots
docs.text:
Eventify rebuilds an aggregate from its events. Add a snapshot when a long history makes that too expensive.

@AggregateRoot("order")
@EnableSnapshotting(threshold = 500)
public class Order { ... }

Eventify saves a snapshot after a successful command when the threshold is crossed. Handlers need no special code.

Setting Meaning threshold Take a snapshot after a successful command when the aggregate crosses a multiple of N events. Defaults to 500. deleteEvents Remove events before the snapshot after it is safely stored. Defaults to false.

Keep deleteEvents disabled when you need full audit history or time travel before the snapshot. If events were deleted and a later code change makes the snapshot unreadable, Eventify cannot rebuild that aggregate.

docs.title: Aggregate changes
docs.text:
Raise the aggregate's @Revision when a changed field or @EventSourcingHandler method would produce a different state from the same events.

@AggregateRoot("order")
@Revision(2)
@EnableSnapshotting(threshold = 500)
public class Order { ... }

Old snapshots are then ignored and rebuilt from events when possible.

docs.title: Event upcasting
docs.text:
Upcasters transform old event JSON into the current event shape while reading history. Increase an event's @Revision and add one @Upcaster method per step.

@Revision(2)
public record OrderPlaced(@AggregateId String id, String customer, String channel) {}

public class OrderUpcaster {
    @Upcaster(type = "com.example.OrderPlaced", revision = 1)
    public JsonNode addChannel(ObjectNode json) {
        json.put("channel", "web");
        return json;
    }
}

Register the upcaster like any other handler. Keep old upcasters: older events may still need every step in the chain.

docs.title: Annotation Reference
docs.text: Annotation Use @Topic("...") Topic for a command or event type. @AggregateId The aggregate identifier field on a command, event or aggregate. @AggregateRoot("...") Stable name of an aggregate type. @CommandHandler Decides which events a command produces. @EventSourcingHandler Produces the next aggregate state from an event. @EventHandler Reacts to a published event outside the aggregate; may return commands to send. @EnableSnapshotting Enables periodic snapshots. @Revision(n) Version of an event schema or aggregate snapshot shape. @Upcaster(type, revision) Migrates an older event shape while reading it. @Priority(n) Execution order of matching @EventHandler methods; higher runs first. @Timestamp Injects a message timestamp. @MessageId Injects a message id. @MetadataValue("key") Injects one metadata value. @Sequence Injects the event's position in its aggregate's history.

docs.title: Command Gateway
docs.text:
Use CommandGateway at your application boundary to send a command and receive its outcome.

CommandGateway gateway = CommandGateway.builder()
    .producerConfig(producerConfig)
    .replyTopic("orders.replies")
    .build();

Create the reply topic first: the gateway needs it to start.

docs.title: Send a command
docs.text:
CompletableFuture<List<Event>> result = gateway.send(
    new PlaceOrder("order-1", "Ada")
);

List<Event> completed = gateway.sendAndWait(
    new PlaceOrder("order-1", "Ada")
);

send is asynchronous. sendAndWait blocks until a result or timeout (one minute by default). A rejected command completes exceptionally with CommandExecutionException. A timeout means no result arrived in time; the command may still have been handled.

docs.title: Schedule a command
docs.text:
ScheduleToken token = gateway.schedule(new CancelOrderIfUnpaid("order-1"), Instant.now().plus(Duration.ofMinutes(30))).join();

gateway.cancel(token);

The command is handled at that time, not earlier. The future completes once the command is scheduled, not when it is handled.

Keep the token to cancel the command. A command that was already handled can't be cancelled, so let its handler check the state too, for example whether the order is already paid.

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text:
Wrap a payload in Command when you want to add metadata.

gateway.send(Command.builder()
    .payload(new PlaceOrder("order-1", "Ada"))
    .metadata(Metadata.of("tenant", "acme"))
    .build());

Eventify passes command metadata to produced events and adds correlation and causation ids.

Close the gateway when the application shuts down; it implements AutoCloseable.

docs.title: Eventify Console
docs.text: Eventify Console is an ops UI for inspecting aggregates, events and command outcomes.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
docker run -p 8080:8080 ghcr.io/alikelleci/eventify-console:latest

Open http://localhost:8080.

docs.title: Connect an application
docs.text:
Add the client dependency and register the plugin.

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.alikelleci</groupId>
    <artifactId>eventify-console-client</artifactId>
    <version>x.y.z</version>
</dependency>

Eventify eventify = Eventify.builder()
    .streamsConfig(config)
    .registerPlugin(EventifyConsoleClient.builder()
        .url("http://localhost:8080")
        .build())
    .build();

Connected applications appear automatically. The console can show stored events, aggregate state and recent command outcomes.

docs.title: Secure it
docs.text:
For production, protect both the UI and application connection:

  • Set EVENTIFY_CONSOLE_APPTOKEN on the console and pass the same value with .token(...) in each client.
  • Configure OpenID Connect with EVENTIFY_CONSOLE_OIDC_ISSUERURI, EVENTIFY_CONSOLE_OIDC_CLIENTID and EVENTIFY_CONSOLE_OIDC_CLIENTSECRET.

Register <scheme>://<console-address>/login/oauth2/code/sso as the redirect URI with your identity provider; use HTTPS in production.

docs.title: Domain Modeling
docs.text:
An aggregate is one consistency boundary. Give it a stable name and an identifier; commands and events for that aggregate carry the same id.

@AggregateRoot("order")
public record Order(@AggregateId String id, String customer, String trackingNumber) {}

Use an immutable aggregate. The name in @AggregateRoot identifies stored history, so keep it stable.

docs.title: Commands and events
docs.text:
Commands express intent; events express facts. Both need exactly one @AggregateId field. Group related types under one @Topic.

@Topic("commands.order")
public interface OrderCommand {
    record Place(@AggregateId String id, String customer) implements OrderCommand {}
    record Ship(@AggregateId String id, String trackingNumber) implements OrderCommand {}
}

@Topic("events.order")
public interface OrderEvent {
    record Placed(@AggregateId String id, String customer) implements OrderEvent {}
    record Shipped(@AggregateId String id, String trackingNumber) implements OrderEvent {}
}

Use Bean Validation annotations on command fields when input validation belongs with the command.

docs.title: Rules of thumb
docs.text:
• Choose event names in past tense: OrderPlaced, not PlaceOrder.
  • Put business time in the event payload; Eventify's timestamp is recording time.
  • Never change an existing event's meaning. Add an upcaster when its shape changes.
  • A removed aggregate is represented by an event whose @EventSourcingHandler method returns null.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: Add Eventify, define your domain, register handlers and start the application.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: Java 17 or later and access to an Apache Kafka cluster.

docs.title: Add the dependency
docs.text:
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.alikelleci</groupId>
    <artifactId>eventify-core</artifactId>
    <version>x.y.z</version>
</dependency>

docs.title: Define a small domain
docs.text:
@Topic("commands.order")
public record PlaceOrder(@AggregateId String id, String customer) {}

@Topic("events.order")
public record OrderPlaced(@AggregateId String id, String customer) {}

@AggregateRoot("order")
public record Order(@AggregateId String id, String customer) {}

docs.title: Add the behavior
docs.text:
public class OrderHandler {
    @CommandHandler
    public OrderPlaced handle(PlaceOrder command, Order state) {
        if (state != null) throw new ValidationException("Order already exists.");
        return new OrderPlaced(command.id(), command.customer());
    }

    @EventSourcingHandler
    public Order handle(OrderPlaced event, Order state) {
        return new Order(event.id(), event.customer());
    }
}

The command handler decides which event to record. The @EventSourcingHandler method is the only place that changes aggregate state.

docs.title: Start Eventify
docs.text:
Properties config = new Properties();
config.put(StreamsConfig.APPLICATION_ID_CONFIG, "orders");
config.put(StreamsConfig.BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS_CONFIG, "localhost:9092");

Eventify eventify = Eventify.builder()
    .streamsConfig(config)
    .registerHandler(new OrderHandler())
    .build();

eventify.start();

Create the topics first: each command topic with its .results and .scheduled topic (commands.order, commands.order.results, commands.order.scheduled), and each event topic. Eventify needs them.

Use the aggregate id as the key when sending a command. Command Gateway is the simplest way to do that.

docs.title: Spring Boot
docs.text: Using Spring Boot? Add eventify-spring-boot-starter instead and see Spring Boot: it registers your handler beans and starts Eventify for you.

docs.title: Handlers
docs.text: Handlers are plain Java methods. Register the object that contains them with Eventify.

docs.title: Handle a command
docs.text:
A command handler receives a command and the current aggregate state. Return one event, a list of events, or no event.

@CommandHandler
public OrderEvent handle(ShipOrder command, Order state) {
    if (state == null) throw new ValidationException("Order does not exist.");
    if (state.trackingNumber() != null) return null;
    return new OrderShipped(command.id(), command.trackingNumber());
}

Throw an exception to reject the command. A successful command with no events is allowed.

docs.title: Apply an event
docs.text:
An event-sourcing handler returns the next aggregate state.

@EventSourcingHandler
public Order handle(OrderShipped event, Order state) {
    return new Order(state.id(), state.customer(), event.trackingNumber());
}

Keep @EventSourcingHandler methods deterministic and side-effect free. They run whenever Eventify rebuilds state. Return null to remove an aggregate.

Events without a matching method are recorded but do not change aggregate state.

docs.title: React to an event
docs.text:
Use @EventHandler for work outside the aggregate, such as projections or notifications.

@EventHandler
public void handle(OrderPlaced event) {
    ordersView.insert(event.id(), event.customer());
}

Make side effects idempotent. A handler may run again after recovery.

An exception in an event handler stops Eventify, including command handling. Put work that can fail, such as sending mail, in a Spring listener or a separate Eventify instance.

docs.title: Send a command from an event
docs.text:
An event handler can return one command, a list of commands, or null. Eventify sends them to their @Topic in the same transaction as reading the event. It passes the event's metadata to the commands and sets the event as their cause.

@EventHandler
public RequestPayment handle(OrderPlaced event) {
    return new RequestPayment(event.paymentId(), event.id(), event.amount());
}

Use this to let one aggregate's event lead to a command for another. The aggregate keeps the state; the handler only decides which command follows.

Return a Command to add metadata of your own, or Scheduled.of(...) to have the command handled later. A list can mix them.

@EventHandler
public List<Object> handle(OrderPlaced event, @Timestamp Instant placedAt) {
    return List.of(
        Command.builder().payload(new ReserveStock(event.id())).metadata(Metadata.of("priority", "high")).build(),
        Scheduled.of(new CancelOrderIfUnpaid(event.id()), placedAt.plus(Duration.ofMinutes(30))));
}

Take the time from the event, so a replay schedules the same time.

docs.title: Available message values
docs.text:
Besides the payload and aggregate state, handlers can receive:

Parameter Value @AggregateRoot type Current state; allowed in command and event-sourcing handlers, required in command handlers Metadata All message metadata @Timestamp Instant Message timestamp @MessageId String Message id @MetadataValue("key") String One metadata value @Sequence long Event's position in its aggregate's history, starting at 1; not in command handlers

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text: Use @Priority only when multiple @EventHandler methods handle the same event. Higher values run first.

docs.title: Spring Boot
docs.text:
The starter registers your handler beans and starts Eventify with the application. It needs Spring Boot 4.

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.alikelleci</groupId>
    <artifactId>eventify-spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
    <version>x.y.z</version>
</dependency>

docs.title: Set it up
docs.text:
Expose an Eventify bean and make your handler classes Spring beans. The EventifyBuilder the starter injects already holds every bean with handler or upcaster methods.

@Bean
Eventify eventify(EventifyBuilder builder) {
    return builder.streamsConfig(config).build();
}

@Component
public class OrderHandler {
    @CommandHandler
    public OrderPlaced handle(PlaceOrder command, Order state) { ... }
}

Handler beans can use Spring as usual: inject dependencies, or add @Transactional.

docs.title: Health
docs.text: With Spring Boot Actuator, the health endpoint has an eventify entry. It is down when Eventify has stopped.

docs.title: Spring listeners
docs.text:
With Spring Kafka on the classpath, the starter can also deserialize Eventify events for @KafkaListener methods. Select its container factory:

@KafkaListener(topics = "events.order", groupId = "orders-view",
               containerFactory = "eventifyListenerContainerFactory")
public void handle(OrderPlaced event, @Timestamp Instant placedAt, @Sequence long sequence) {
    ordersView.insert(event.id(), event.customer(), placedAt);
}

A listener method takes the same parameters as an @EventHandler, or the whole Event. Only committed events arrive; events of a class the application doesn't have are skipped.

A listener method for one event type fails on the other types on its topic. For a topic with several types, take Event, or put @KafkaListener on a class with a @KafkaHandler method per type and one with isDefault = true for the rest.

Use this when a projection should have its own lifecycle and error handling; command handling always uses @CommandHandler.

docs.title: Read events yourself
docs.text:
To read events in a projection of your own, e.g. a Kafka Streams application, inject the starter's EventSerde bean. It reads events with the same upcasters as Eventify.

builder.stream("events.order", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), eventSerde));

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
eventify-test tests your handlers without a broker: AggregateFixture for aggregates, EventHandlerFixture for event handlers.

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.alikelleci</groupId>
    <artifactId>eventify-test</artifactId>
    <version>x.y.z</version>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>

docs.title: Aggregates
docs.text:
Given the aggregate's past events, when a command arrives, then expect its events, its rejection or its new state.

AggregateFixture<Order> fixture = AggregateFixture.of(Order.class, new OrderHandler());

@Test
void placesAnOrder() {
    fixture.when(new PlaceOrder("order-1", "Ada"))
        .expectEvents(new OrderPlaced("order-1", "Ada"))
        .expectState(order -> assertThat(order.customer()).isEqualTo("Ada"));
}

@Test
void cancelsAPlacedOrder() {
    fixture.given(new OrderPlaced("order-1", "Ada"))
        .when(new CancelOrder("order-1"))
        .expectEvents(new OrderCancelled("order-1"));
}

@Test
void rejectsAnUnknownOrder() {
    fixture.when(new CancelOrder("order-1"))
        .expectRejection(OrderNotFoundException.class);
}
Expectation Passes when expectSuccess() The command was accepted expectEvents(...) The command was accepted with exactly these events, in this order expectNoEvents() The command was accepted without events expectRejection() The command was rejected expectRejection(Exception.class) The command was rejected by this exception, as the root cause expectRejection(Exception.class, "message") The same, with exactly this message expectState(order -> ...) Your assertions pass on the aggregate after the command

Good to know:

  • given(...) takes the events that already happened; leave it out for a new aggregate. when(...) takes the command you test.
  • Pass all handlers of the aggregate, also when they are in separate classes: AggregateFixture.of(Order.class, new OrderCommandHandler(), new OrderEventSourcingHandler()). Without event-sourcing handlers there is no state.
  • The state is null before the aggregate is created and after it is removed.
  • Events are compared with equals: use records or classes with equals, such as Lombok's @Value.
  • For your own assertions: events(), state(), result() and cause() ("Exception: message").

docs.title: Event handlers
docs.text:
When an event arrives, then expect the commands its handlers send now or schedule.

import static io.github.alikelleci.eventify.test.EventHandlerFixture.after;

EventHandlerFixture fixture = EventHandlerFixture.of(new PaymentHandler());

@Test
void requestsPaymentAndCancelsWhenUnpaid() {
    fixture.when(new OrderPlaced("order-1", "Ada"))
        .expectCommands(new RequestPayment("order-1"))
        .expectScheduled(after(Duration.ofMinutes(30), new CancelUnpaidOrder("order-1")));
}

@Test
void failsForALostOrder() {
    fixture.when(new OrderLost("order-1"))
        .expectFailure(IllegalStateException.class);
}
Expectation Passes when expectSuccess() The event was handled expectCommands(...) Exactly these commands were sent now; expectCommands() for none expectScheduled(...) Exactly these commands were scheduled, at these times expectNoCommands() No commands were sent or scheduled expectFailure() A handler failed, and none of the commands were sent expectFailure(Exception.class) A handler failed by this exception, as the root cause expectFailure(Exception.class, "message") The same, with exactly this message

Good to know:

  • after(duration, command) expects the command that long after the event's timestamp. For a fixed time, use Scheduled.of(command, time). Pass all scheduled commands to one expectScheduled(...).
  • The order of commands is checked per topic.
  • Register only event handlers: test command handlers with an AggregateFixture.
  • For your own assertions: commands(), scheduled(), sent() (with metadata) and cause() ("Exception: message").

An event handler without commands, such as a projection, is tested the same way. Give it a fake to write to:

InMemoryOrderOverview overview = new InMemoryOrderOverview();

EventHandlerFixture.of(new OrderOverviewProjection(overview))
    .when(new OrderPlaced("order-1", "Ada"))
    .expectNoCommands();

assertThat(overview.find("order-1").status()).isEqualTo("placed");

docs.title: For both fixtures
docs.text:
• A failed expectation throws an AssertionError, so it works with any test framework.
  • Every when(...) starts from scratch, so one fixture can serve all tests of a class.
  • Expectations take payloads, such as new OrderPlaced(...), not a Command or Event. To check metadata, use result() or sent().
  • When your application builds Eventify with its own objectMapper(...), give the fixture the same one: AggregateFixture.of(...).withObjectMapper(objectMapper).
  • For metadata on the command or event in when(...), pass a Command or Event instead of the payload. An Event needs an aggregate type and sequence; any value will do:
// AggregateFixture
fixture.when(Command.builder().payload(new CancelOrder("order-1"))
    .metadata(Metadata.of("user", "ada")).build());

// EventHandlerFixture
fixture.when(Event.builder().aggregateType("order").sequence(1)
    .payload(new OrderPaid("order-1")).metadata(Metadata.of("user", "ada")).build());

docs.title: The complete flow
docs.text:
To test how aggregates and event handlers work together, use Kafka Streams' TopologyTestDriver yourself. It's in eventify-test too, or add org.apache.kafka:kafka-streams-test-utils.

Properties testConfig = new Properties();
testConfig.put(StreamsConfig.APPLICATION_ID_CONFIG, "orders-test");
testConfig.put(StreamsConfig.BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS_CONFIG, "dummy:9092");

Eventify eventify = Eventify.builder()
    .streamsConfig(testConfig)
    .registerHandler(new OrderHandler())
    .build();

try (TopologyTestDriver driver = new TopologyTestDriver(eventify.topology())) {
    var commands = driver.createInputTopic(
        "commands.order", new StringSerializer(), new CommandSerde().serializer());
    var results = driver.createOutputTopic(
        "commands.order.results", new StringDeserializer(), new CommandResultSerde().deserializer());
    var events = driver.createOutputTopic(
        "events.order", new StringDeserializer(), new EventSerde().deserializer());

    Command command = Command.builder().payload(new PlaceOrder("order-1", "Ada")).build();
    commands.pipeInput(command.getAggregateId(), command);

    assertThat(results.readValue()).isInstanceOf(CommandResult.Success.class);
    assertThat(events.readValue().getPayload()).isEqualTo(new OrderPlaced("order-1", "Ada"));
}
